explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. They had heard the antichrist is coming, and the writer says, "so now many antichrists have appeared" (1 John 2:18). Many! That's like reaching for one cookie and finding the whole tray already out. And he says that's how they know it is the last hour (1 John 2:18).

Nobody gets captured in these verses, friend. The writer says "many antichrists have appeared" (1 John 2:18), and that's the news he gives. Not one handcuff anywhere in the passage. It's just a heads-up that they've already shown up.

The writer never gives a name here. He says "many antichrists have appeared" (1 John 2:18), and many is a crowd, not one famous face. I think a list of names would need a second page and a bigger pencil. So the news is the number, not a name.

True. The writer says, "They went out from us, but they did not belong to us" (1 John 2:19). So they didn't wander in from somewhere else, they walked out from among the believers. And the walking out is what showed it, because he says, "their departure made it clear that none of them belonged to us." (1 John 2:19)

It's the other way around, friend. The writer says, "They went out from us, but they did not belong to us" (1 John 2:19). They started out among the believers and then left. Easy to flip when you read fast, like putting the stamp on before the dough is rolled out.

Remained is the word. The writer says, "For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us" (1 John 2:19). They left, and he says that made it clear none of them belonged (1 John 2:19). A cookie that belongs in the box stays in the box, friend.

Worshiping isn't the word in this verse. The writer says that if they had belonged, they would have "remained with us" (1 John 2:19). It's all about staying put, not about what they'd be doing once they stayed.

Serving sounds nice, like a tray of warm cookies, but it isn't the word here. The writer says they would have "remained with us" (1 John 2:19). Staying is what that line is about. If they had belonged, they would have stuck around.

All! The writer says, "You, however, have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth" (1 John 2:20). Not a lucky few, and not just the sharpest ones. Everybody walks out of that kitchen with a cookie.

Most would leave somebody standing at the edge, and the writer doesn't do that. He says "all of you know the truth" (1 John 2:20). Picture a batch where most of the cookies got chocolate chips. Somebody's holding a plain one right now, and he is NOT happy.

Some makes a short guest list, and the writer isn't keeping one. He says "all of you know the truth" (1 John 2:20). The anointing from the Holy One belongs to every one of those believers (1 John 2:20). Nobody gets left at the door with an empty box.

The writer says the opposite: "no lie comes from the truth" (1 John 2:21). An oven doesn't blow out cold air, and the truth doesn't hand out lies. He also says he wrote to them because they have the truth (1 John 2:21).

False is right. The writer says "no lie comes from the truth" (1 John 2:21). You can't pull a lie out of the truth any more than you can pull a cookie out of an empty jar. And he says he isn't writing because they lack the truth, but because they have it (1 John 2:21).

explanations.answer: Whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ
explanations.explanation: That's the one. The writer asks, "Who is the liar, if it is not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ?" (1 John 2:22). He asks it and answers it in the same breath. No suspense, friend, the timer didn't even start. Then he adds, "This is the antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son." (1 John 2:22)

Sabbath rest never comes up in these verses. The writer's answer is "the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ" (1 John 2:22). I get the guess, though. It sounds official, like a rule posted on a bakery door.

Doubting the prophets isn't what he says here. His answer is "the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ" (1 John 2:22). That's the person he calls the liar. He also says this person denies the Father and the Son (1 John 2:22). Sounds scholarly, I'll give you that.

It's the opposite, friend. The writer says, "Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father" (1 John 2:23). Father and Son go together in these lines, like me and my mustache. You don't get one without the other. Then he flips it: "but whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well." (1 John 2:23)

False, and the writer is plain about it: "Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father" (1 John 2:23). Then comes the other side: "but whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well." (1 John 2:23) Son and Father go as a pair in these lines, like a cookie jar and its lid.

True. The writer says, "As for you, let what you have heard from the beginning remain in you" (1 John 2:24). Let it stay put, like the smell of a fresh batch that won't leave the kitchen. And he adds, "If it does, you will also remain in the Son and in the Father." (1 John 2:24)

He does tell them that, friend. The writer says, "let what you have heard from the beginning remain in you" (1 John 2:24). Nobody's asking them to swap the recipe for a shinier one. If it remains, he says, "you will also remain in the Son and in the Father" (1 John 2:24).

Eternal life. The writer says, "And this is the promise that He Himself made to us: eternal life." (1 John 2:25) He says the promise was made to us, so he's counting himself in right alongside the believers. That's a promise I'd frame and hang over my ovens.

A land isn't what this verse names. The writer says the promise is "eternal life" (1 John 2:25). I've got a whole cookie planet and I love it, but that's not the promise he's talking about here. It's one that "He Himself made to us" (1 John 2:25).

Peace with their enemies isn't in this verse. The writer names "eternal life" as the promise "He Himself made to us" (1 John 2:25). Peace sounds lovely, and I'd take a quiet kitchen any day. But the verse names something else.

explanations.answer: Those who are trying to deceive them
explanations.explanation: That's who. The writer says, "I have written these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you." (1 John 2:26) He's writing about them. Think of a cookie jar with COOKIES on the label and nothing but rubber bands inside. That's the kind of trick he's pointing at.

explanations.answer: Those who are new to the faith
explanations.explanation: New believers aren't who he names here. He says he wrote "about those who are trying to deceive you" (1 John 2:26). The people in this verse are the ones doing the deceiving. Fresh faces are always welcome in my bakery, but they aren't the topic of this line.

explanations.answer: Those who are suffering for Jesus
explanations.explanation: Suffering isn't mentioned in this verse. The writer says he wrote "about those who are trying to deceive you" (1 John 2:26). Hard times are real and I'd never joke about them, but they aren't what this line is about.

explanations.answer: Remain in Him as they were taught
explanations.explanation: That's it. The writer says, "just as His true and genuine anointing teaches you about all things, so remain in Him as you have been taught" (1 John 2:27). No new assignment and no big sprint. He also says the anointing remains in them and they do not need anyone to teach them (1 John 2:27).

explanations.answer: Go bring back the ones who left
explanations.explanation: Going after the ones who left isn't in these verses. The writer says they went out from the believers (1 John 2:19), but his closing instruction is "remain in Him as you have been taught" (1 John 2:27). The job here is to stay, not to chase. I'd be a terrible chaser anyway, since I can't even step off my gold base.

Teaching newer believers isn't what this verse tells them to do. The writer says to "remain in Him as you have been taught" (1 John 2:27). He even says they do not need anyone to teach them, and that His anointing teaches them about all things (1 John 2:27). Put the clipboard down, friend.
